reviewHtml:
Abraham Ortuño Perez is a doting uncle; he also has a flair for seeing the world from a child’s eye level. For spring that meant magnifying, shrinking and turning things upside down. Setting the tone on the runway was a table stacked with china and a floral arrangement, the whole thing flipped teacups-down with a bird’s nest holding golden eggs perched atop one leg. On the opposite side of the room stood an upturned coatrack and chairs arranged higgledy-piggledy, perhaps a wink at the chair-dresses he sent down the runway last season.

Backstage before the show, the designer explained that he had three points of departure: Studio Ghibli’s The Secret World of Arrietty; the Sylvanian Families he has been collecting with his young relatives (those inspired the tactile velvets, wide-wale corduroys and lamés) and Alice’s mushroom-eating adventures in the Wonderland. But he leavened the vibe with pointed commentary. “I figured since the world is so fucked up right now, we might as well turn everything upside down,” Ortuño Perez quipped.

Down the rabbit hole, silhouettes duly came out flipped head to toe, literally: patent red shoes sat on wigs (a nod to Elsa Schiaparelli), lips were drawn upside-down, skirts became bustiers, and tresses flopped about on shoes (it’s worth noting that those were styled by hair guru Charlie Le Mindu). Ortuño Perez also played with proportions and print. There was a blown-up gingham slipped under an overall/skirt hybrid—gamely worn by pop star friend Hannah Diamond (who also did the soundtrack), all but incognito in pink to match her hair. A trippy ’70s mushroom print was seemingly fused with a black slip dress. Statement pieces like a “forest fairy” purple lamé/trench hybrid overshadowed quieter ones, like corduroy jackets in khaki or cream, that could well turn out to have serious commercial appeal.

For the finale, Ortuño Perez sent out a couple of “forest bed” leaf dresses made of boned, wired, printed and hand-cut duchesse satin. Those were a tribute to his new life as a part-time resident of Mallorca, courtesy of his collaboration with Camper, and the footwear brand’s Pelotas cropped up here with red laces, a leaf and an added bow.

“I love to wear quiet fashion but I always have to mix it with something crazy,” the designer offered. “It’s not finished unless there is something special.” Speaking of which, those wig pumps aren’t just a show trick. Ortuño Perez fully intends to produce them—even if it’s just three pairs at a time. Creating such moments is important, he added. “Strong pieces are what keep fashion alive.” Not all of them were practical and some were downright silly, but this outing amounted to a whole lot of fun.
